prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The map consistently places the striped-shirt person about 0.5–1.2 m in front of the camera wearer, initially left-of-centre and leaning over a waist-high wall, then shifting toward the centre/right and becoming partly cropped at the far-right edge; the bright upper body and arms indicate they are nearer than the wall interior and ground. The wall rim is roughly 0.5–1 m away and within the camera wearer’s arm’s reach, while the wall’s inner surface and vegetation/ground beyond it appear progressively darker and therefore farther, approximately 1.5–4+ m away. Bright lower-edge regions in several frames correspond to the camera wearer’s nearby arm or body, while the person, wall, and frame boundaries occlude much of the space behind them. Depth makes near–far layering clearer than RGB, but distances are only rough: brightness changes abruptly on the person and wall, the far background collapses into similar dark values, and some bright edge regions appear erroneous.
descriptions.segmentation: The map isolates the principal nearby person across all five frames, showing their silhouette leaning from the upper-left/centre toward the wall and then moving to the right edge, about 0.5–1.2 m from the camera wearer. Additional partial masks near the lower edge in frames 2, 3, and 5 indicate close, cropped body parts approximately 0–0.5 m from the camera, although the large frame-2 mask is incorrectly labelled “dog” and the lower masks labelled “person” have uncertain ownership. The masks expose occlusion boundaries and show that the main person’s torso and legs block the wall and ground behind them, while their upper body is partly cut off by the top edge and increasingly by the right edge in the final frame. Segmentation clarifies which visible regions belong to separate foreground instances, but it provides no direct metric distance, omits the wall, hose, plants, and block, and contains obvious class and boundary errors, so facing direction and gaze cannot be determined reliably from it.
descriptions.pose: The pose map is entirely black in all five frames, so it supplies no detected body or hand skeletons and therefore no joint-based evidence for facing direction, gaze, limb orientation, reach, or motion. Using only the aligned RGB context, a nearby person remains in front of the wearer and leans over the wall before shifting rightward, but none of that spatial structure is represented by this map. The absence of landmarks also prevents separating the camera wearer’s partly visible lower-edge body from the other person or measuring their relative positions and distances. Thus the pose output adds nothing beyond RGB here and is unreliable, likely because bodies and hands are heavily cropped, occluded, or viewed from angles that defeated detection.
